overview.text: Protein folding is the process in which a newly made chain of amino acids takes on a particular three-dimensional shape. The chain’s amino-acid sequence influences that shape, while interactions among parts of the chain help it become compact and organized. Folding can begin while the chain is still being made and continue afterward. The resulting shape is important because it helps determine what the protein can do. Some proteins fold without assistance; others are helped by cellular proteins called chaperones, which can reduce incorrect folding or clumping. Folding is not simply a random search through every possible shape: proteins reach their structures through pathways shaped by their chemistry.

key_facts.text: A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; folding may start during translation and continue afterward.
The amino-acid sequence helps specify a protein’s three-dimensional shape, though the chemical environment also matters.
In many proteins, water-avoiding (hydrophobic) amino-acid side chains tend to cluster inside, helping the chain become compact.
Some proteins fold spontaneously, while chaperones help others fold and can prevent them from aggregating.
A protein’s folded shape is important to its function; abnormal temperature or pH can interfere with correct folding.
